nodes.label: Korean Agglutinative Stem+Ending Morphology
nodes.rationale: Verbs/adjectives = stem + pre-final ending(s) + final ending; stems never stand alone. Vowel-based vs. consonant-based stems condition allomorphy across nearly every subsequent ending, paralleled functionally (not phonologically) to Hungarian vowel-harmony-driven allomorphy and Finnish stem alternation documented elsewhere in this project.

nodes.label: Korean Six-Level Honorific/Speech-Level System
nodes.rationale: Flagship cross-book finding for Korean: six ranked speech levels (deferential, polite, blunt, familiar, intimate, plain), each with its own full paradigm of declarative/interrogative/imperative/propositive endings, encoding social relationship (not propositional content) directly in verb morphology. Byon (001) documents the full 6-level table and notes blunt/familiar are declining among younger speakers; Intermediate Korean (003) documents intimate/plain in depth; Continuing Korean (005/006) documents productive honorific stacking, over-honorification judgments, and the full Plain/Intimate Style system including its role as the base for quoted speech.

nodes.label: Humble Verb 뵙-/뵈- (humbly see/meet)
nodes.rationale: Humble-register verb with its own irregular conjugation (뵈도/뵈어도, not the expected *뵈워도); 찾아 뵈- 'call on someone esteemed' contrasts with plain 찾아 가-.

nodes.label: Humble Suppletive Verb Set
nodes.rationale: Closed set of lexically distinct humble-register verbs (not derived by suffixation) used when the speaker's own action affects an esteemed referent — e.g. 말씀(을) 드리- 'tell (humble)', 뵙-/뵈- 'humbly see/meet' with irregular conjugation, 찾아 뵈- vs. plain 찾아 가-. Parallels the honorific-direction suppletive pairs (먹다→잡수시다, 자다→주무시다, 있다→계시다) documented in Basic Korean Unit 25.

nodes.label: Intimate Style (반말)
nodes.rationale: Formed by stripping polite 요 from Polite Style forms (with a documented list of irregular exceptions); used among close intimates and toward children. Intermediate Korean Unit 1 independently documents the same level as one ending covering all four sentence types, contrasted with Plain Style's per-sentence-type endings.

nodes.label: Seven Irregular Predicate Classes (ㄷ/ㅂ/ㅅ/ㅎ/르/ㄹ/으)
nodes.rationale: Unit 19's seven irregular-predicate classes, each with a full paradigm and a regular-contrast set illustrating the sound-change pattern that distinguishes irregular from regular stems of the same shape.

nodes.label: Native/Sino-Korean/Loanword Lexical Stratification
nodes.rationale: Korean nouns derive from three sources: native Korean (~35%), Sino-Korean (~60%, historically borrowed from Chinese), and loanwords (~5%, mostly English) — introduced in Unit 3 as a word-formation/derivation topic; the checklist's summary of established/008 (outside this chunk) later develops this into 'the single richest register-generating mechanism found' for the corpus overall.

nodes.label: Plain Style (반말체)
nodes.rationale: Lowest/plainest of the six speech levels; functions as (a) neutral written register (newspapers, textbooks), (b) spoken register between intimates or superior-to-inferior, and (c) the foundational base form for the entire direct/indirect quotation system (Lesson 27). Statement/question/command/suggestion endings each differ by verb class (descriptive vs. processive).

nodes.label: Direct/Indirect Quotation System Built on Plain Style
nodes.rationale: Lesson 27 builds the full direct/indirect quotation system on top of Plain Style forms, with quoted statements/questions/suggestions/commands each downgraded to their Plain Style base ending, plus a suppletive-verb quotation rule (달라(고) 하- for quoting 주세요 'give me'). Sibling file established/004 (Intermediate Korean Unit 24) independently documents the same structural pattern: indirect quotation structurally downgrades any quoted utterance to the plain speech level, with colloquial ~대요/~래요/~(으)래요/~재요 contractions.
nodes.norm_label: direct/indirect quotation system built on plain style

nodes.label: SOV / Context-Oriented / Big-to-Small Word-Order Typology
nodes.rationale: Korean is verb-final with comparatively free word order (case particles fix grammatical role); context-oriented (subject/object routinely dropped when recoverable); and general-to-specific ordering (family name before given name, address/date ordering reversed from English).

nodes.label: Subject-Honorific Suffix -(으)시
nodes.rationale: Pre-final verb suffix marking deference toward the sentence's SUBJECT, orthogonal to which speech-level ending (addressee-oriented) is chosen; the two systems are independent and can combine (e.g. intimate-level sentence with honorific subject suffix).

nodes.label: Suppletive Honorific Pair 먹다/잡수시다 (eat)
nodes.rationale: One of a closed set of suppletive honorific verbs (with 자다→주무시다 'sleep', 있다→계시다 'exist/stay') that already lexically contain the -시 honorific and do not additionally take the -(으)시 suffix.

nodes.label: Hangul Design & Historical Vowel Harmony
nodes.rationale: Hangul (21 vowels + 19 consonants) invented 1443 under King Sejong; bright/dark/neutral vowel-harmony grouping is presented as the historical reason certain double-vowel glyphs don't exist, not as a productive modern rule (contrast fully synchronically active Hungarian vowel harmony documented elsewhere in this project).

nodes.label: Byon's Minimal-Pair Register Example (어제 우리/저희 모임에...)
nodes.rationale: Byon's own worked minimal pair contrasting intimate/plain register (plain 우리, no honorific suffix, intimate ending -어) against formal/deferential register (humble 저희, honorific suffix -시, deferential ending -습니다) for the same referential meaning — illustrating the Unit 2 claim that 'how an utterance is said is more important than what is said.'
nodes.norm_label: byon's minimal-pair register example (어제 우리/저희 모임에...)

nodes.label: -거든요 as a Politeness/Conversation-Management Device
nodes.rationale: §16.6: the text explicitly frames -거든요 as a politeness strategy ('grease on the skids') that keeps conversation moving and invites a minimal acknowledging response, independent of its literal 'because' meaning — an explicit source-internal register/pragmatics annotation rather than a purely semantic gloss.

nodes.label: +36266 Codepoint-Offset Font-Substitution Cipher (Wave 1 PDF gotcha)
nodes.rationale: Intermediate Korean's embedded Korean font (Batang-KSCms-UHC-H-Identity-H, CID-keyed, no ToUnicode CMap) decodes through pdftotext/PyMuPDF into unrelated CJK glyphs — not OCR garbling but a fixed, consistent substitution: real Hangul = chr(ord(extracted_char) + 36266) whenever that lands in the Hangul Syllables block (U+AC00-U+D7A3), with a small blacklist of typographic characters (curly quotes, dashes, ellipsis) excluded to avoid false positives. Verified against 15+ known word/gloss pairs across widely separated pages in both 003 and 004 (the two halves of Intermediate Korean), and independently re-discovered in Using Korean (established/008, outside this chunk). This decode methodology is the rationale for why 003/004 carry no vision-reading confidence flags despite being 'clean text layer' PDFs — the decode is a character remap of machine-extracted text, not a vision reading.

nodes.label: Speaker Self-Effacement Rule (-(으)시 never applies to speaker)
nodes.rationale: Speakers never apply the subject-honorific suffix -(으)시 to their own actions: 어디에 가세요? (honorific, asked of addressee) is answered 집에 가요 (no honorific on the speaker's own action). Flagged by the source file as worth comparing against any later slang register that violates or plays with self-honorification as a marked departure from this baseline norm.
nodes.norm_label: speaker self-effacement rule (-(으)시 never applies to speaker)

nodes.label: Productive Honorific Stacking & Over-Honorification Judgment
nodes.rationale: Continuing Korean §17.1 documents up to six mathematically possible honorific/negative combinations on a single sensory-verb compound; the most fully-stacked form is explicitly called by the source 'a bit too fancy for everyday use' — a rare case of a grammar reference directly annotating a register judgment on a specific derived form, flagged as directly relevant to slang/register mechanics synthesis.

nodes.label: Non-Embedded Korean Font Forcing Vision-Reading (Basic Korean gotcha)
nodes.rationale: Basic Korean's Korean-language font (Batang-KSCms-UHC-H-Identity-H, pdffonts confirms emb:no, Identity-H with no ToUnicode map) is not embedded at all, so extracted Hangul glyphs come out as unrelated Unicode (Sinhala-range) or bare unresolved (cid:NNNN) codes with no stable 1:1 substitution to decode — distinct from the +36266 cipher case, which IS a stable decodable substitution. English text on the same pages extracts cleanly; only Hangul is affected. All Korean content in 001 was vision-read from rendered page images as a result. A follow-up note in 002's header flags that Units 16-25 of the SAME book were later found to have a decodable +36266 text layer after all, raising the open question of whether Units 1-15 could be re-decoded rather than left vision-read.
nodes.norm_label: non-embedded korean font forcing vision-reading (basic korean gotcha)

nodes.label: Blunt/Familiar Speech-Level Decline (Register Obsolescence)
nodes.rationale: Byon explicitly notes speech levels 3 (Blunt) and 4 (Familiar) are declining among younger generations and are deliberately not covered further in the book, which instead focuses on levels 1/2/5/6. Flagged as relevant to sci-fi conlang slang synthesis: a live language can shed whole formality strata over a generation; a designed slang register system could plausibly mirror or invert this kind of stratum-loss.
